newsitem.title: JAPAN: Palladium stock would thwart squeeze - Japan traders.
newsitem.headline: Palladium stock would thwart squeeze - Japan traders.

text.p: Russia's palladium stocks are probably sufficient to thwart any speculative attempt to squeeze the market, Japanese traders said on Friday, adding that current speculative plays were likely to be short-term.

"The funds might aim to squeeze the palladium market by buying tons of palladium, probably on the back of market rumours that Russian stocks of platinum group metals are drying up," an official at a bullion house said. "But I don't think it would be easy, as the palladium market is not that small."
He added that the Russian platinum group metal (PGM) export agency had said Russia held ample palladium stocks to meet world demand through the year 2000.
Nevertheless, Russia's PGM stock levels, still a closely guarded state secret, have long been a mystery to the market and a subject of intense speculation.
The February issue of "Institutional Investor" magazine, published this week, said hedge fund Tiger Management, run by Julian Robertson, had been buying "tons of palladium recently".
"At some point -- I don't know when -- all these people are going to be asking, 'where are we going to get our palladium'," the magazine quoted Robertson as saying. "And the only place will be us."
Tiger Management has about $8 billion under management. One year's global palladium consumption is worth about $825 million at current market prices.
Palladium prices rallied strongly in recent weeks as a prolonged delay in Japan-Russia negotiations for 1997 supply contracts sparked tightness in the spot market and encouraged speculative buying.
Russia and Japan are, respectively, the world's largest producer and consumer of palladium, which is used in electronic components, dental fillings and catalytic converters for cars.
Spot prices surged above $140 an ounce last week to their highest levels in more than 10 months, although they have since retraced. On Friday spot palladium was quoted at $134/$135.
Despite Robertson's reported comments, Japanese traders remained sanguine about the possibility of a long-term speculative squeeze.
One trader said that high storage and financing costs would discourage any attempts to hoard metal.
In addition, the Russians have a long history of boosting palladium sales from their stockpiles whenever prices rise too far, in order to discourage substitution with cheaper metals like nickel.

Indeed, a switch to nickel last year by many Japanese electronics manufacturers, combined with large Japanese inventories, helped spur a slide in palladium prices last fall to two-and-a-half-year lows.
Traders also expected the Russians would have little trouble meeting physical demand once contracts were finally worked out with the Japanese.
At that point, they said, speculators may unload their palladium holdings, causing a slump in prices.

"The comments on hedge fund buying were interesting because they proved that the recent sharp gains were led by fund buying, as physical buyers would not chase the rapid price rises," a trader at a major trading house said.
Added another trader: "If funds such as Tiger Management see that palladium has little scope to rise, those funds, believed to be still holding massive longs, could liquidate their positions."
One trader added that palladium prices could slip to around $125 when the timing of the Japan-Russian talks is decided.
